planting.note: Divide established clumps or set out nursery plants in spring once soil is workable, siting in lean, well-drained soil since rich or wet conditions cause floppy growth and rot.

directions: 'Album' is a pure-white-flowered selection of nettle-leaved mullein, with slender branched spikes studded with small purple-anthered white blooms held above neat rosettes of grey-green, wrinkled leaves. Grow it in lean, gritty, well-drained soil in full sun, since overly fertile or soggy ground shortens its naturally long bloom season and invites crown rot. Deadheading the main spikes after the first flush often encourages a second round of side-branch bloom later in summer. Because seedlings tend to drift back toward the species' pale-yellow color, propagate true 'Album' plants by division or root cuttings rather than relying on self-sown seed.

planting.note: Set out divisions or potted plants in spring in full sun on lean, sharply drained soil, and stake tall spikes in exposed sites.

directions: 'Pink Domino' is a long-cultivated hybrid mullein prized for its tall, stately spires of rose-pink flowers accented by contrasting violet-purple anthers, held above a basal rosette of soft, felted grey-green leaves. It performs best in poor-to-average, fast-draining soil in full sun, where its biennial-leaning but often perennial habit produces the sturdiest flower stalks; overly rich soil tends to make plants floppy and short-lived. Shear spent main spikes back to encourage secondary flowering shoots and extend the display into late summer. As a sterile or near-sterile hybrid, it is propagated by division or root cuttings rather than seed to keep the color true.

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery-grown plants in spring in moisture-retentive, well-drained soil; divide congested clumps every two to three years to maintain vigor.

directions: 'Totally Tangerine' produces an exceptionally long succession of single, soft tangerine-orange flowers on branching, wiry stems that sway well above the semi-evergreen foliage clumps, blooming from late spring deep into autumn with regular deadheading. It thrives in evenly moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade, and resents both waterlogging and prolonged drought. Because this hybrid sets little to no viable seed, it is propagated by division in spring or autumn, which also keeps clumps from becoming overcrowded. Its airy, see-through habit makes it an effective front-to-mid-border plant that weaves attractively among neighboring perennials.

planting.note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant out after frost danger passes, or treat as a self-sowing short-lived perennial in warmer zones.

directions: 'Beaujolais' is a striking selection of the Mediterranean loosestrife grown not for its small flowers but for its dense, dusky wine-purple flower spikes set against silvery-grey, willowy foliage. Unlike the yellow-flowered gooseneck and creeping loosestrifes, this species prefers sharply drained, average soil in full sun and resents heavy, waterlogged ground. In mild climates it behaves as a short-lived perennial that self-sows modestly, while in colder zones it is best grown as a dramatic annual accent for cutting gardens and mixed containers. Pinching young plants once encourages bushier growth and more flowering spikes per plant.

planting.note: Plant grafted or container-grown trees in early spring or fall in full sun on well-drained soil, staking young trees until the central leader is established.

directions: 'Tristis' is one of the oldest named weeping forms of European silver birch, distinguished from the more familiar 'Youngii' by its narrower, more upright and columnar crown topped with long, slender, strongly pendulous branchlets rather than a low, dome-shaped mound. It displays the classic silver birch assets of white, peeling bark and fine-textured, small triangular leaves that turn clear yellow in autumn. Plant in full sun on moist but well-drained, slightly acidic soil, and avoid prolonged drought stress, which predisposes birches to bronze birch borer. Because the graft union is often visible low on the trunk, position and stake young trees carefully so the leader grows straight before the weeping habit fully develops.
